query: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a low volume fraction of stable oxide nanoparticles (e.g., Y2O3) during alloy processing will pin grain boundaries and dislocations in the titanium–nickel high-entropy alloy, thereby retarding grain growth and maintaining enhanced mechanical strength at elevated temperatures compared to the same alloy without the oxide dispersion.
generation.material_initial_state: A titanium–nickel-based high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state produced by powder metallurgy without any intentional dispersoid additions.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled, low-level (~0.5–1 at.%) addition of Y2O3 nanoparticles into the alloy during its processing.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature exposure (e.g., long-term annealing at 800–1000 °C in an inert atmosphere) and/or extreme-environment mechanical testing (e.g., high-temperature microhardness or yield strength measurements).
generation.structural_mediator: Nano-scale oxide dispersoids situated along grain boundaries and within the grains.
generation.mechanism: The Y2O3 particles act as pinning sites that inhibit grain boundary migration and dislocation motion (via Orowan strengthening), thus limiting grain coarsening and preserving a refined microstructure which is linked to higher microhardness and yield strength even after prolonged high-temperature exposure.
generation.predicted_outcome: The oxide-dispersion strengthened alloy will exhibit a slower rate of grain growth and a smaller decrease in hardness and yield strength at elevated temperature compared to the baseline alloy processed without Y2O3.
generation.baseline: The same titanium–nickel high-entropy alloy manufactured by powder metallurgy without Y2O3 nanoparticle additions, which, based on analogous thermal stability studies, shows moderate grain growth and softening under prolonged annealing.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective as long as: (1) the nanoparticle content remains low enough to avoid the formation of separate brittle phases; (2) the processing yields a uniform nanoparticle distribution; and (3) the operating temperature does not exceed the stability range of the oxide phase.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in mechanical properties is uncertain and may depend on nanoparticle dispersion uniformity, interfacial bonding between Y2O3 and the alloy matrix, and long-term stability under cyclic thermal exposures.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the titanium–nickel high-entropy alloy: one set fabricated with the specified addition of Y2O3 nanoparticles and one set processed identically without the nanoparticles. Subject both sets to extended annealing at 900 °C (or within the range of 800–1000 °C) under an inert atmosphere over different time points (e.g., 100, 500, and 1000 hours).
measurements: Yield strength (or related mechanical property tests) at elevated temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y2O3-dispersed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in grain growth and/or a higher retention of hardness and yield strength compared to the baseline samples under the same high-temperature conditions, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

## Abstract
The thermal stability of the grain structure and mechanical properties of the high-entropy two-phase TiCoCrFeMn alloy produced by powder metallurgy, assessed based on microhardness measurements, was analyzed in this work. For this purpose, material obtained via sintering using the U-FAST method was subjected to long-term heating at a temperature of 1000 °C for up to 1000 h in an argon atmosphere. For homogenization times of 1, 10, 20, 50, 100, and 1000 h, grain size changes in the identified phase components of the matrix were assessed, and microhardness measurements were conducted using the Vickers method. It has been shown that the changes in the analyzed parameters are closely correlated with non-monotonic modifications in the chemical composition. It was found that the tested alloy achieved structural stability after 100 h of annealing. A stable grain size was obtained in the BCC solid solution of approximately 2 µm and the two-phase BCC+C14 mixture of roughly 0.4 µm. Long-term heating for up to 1000 h caused the grain structure to grow to 2.7 µm and 0.7 µm, respectively, with a simultaneous decrease in hardness from 1065 HV to 1000 HV.
